lesson.title: Trusting the Numbers: Preparing Standard Solutions
lesson.summary: A standard solution has a precisely known concentration, and understanding how one is prepared, and why some solutions can be trusted immediately while others cannot, is the foundation of reliable titration.
lesson.body:
A standard solution is simply a solution whose concentration is known precisely, and every volumetric analysis calculation you run depends on trusting it. Since molarity is defined as moles of solute per liter of solution, preparing a standard solution in principle just means weighing out a known number of moles of a solute and dissolving it in a volumetric flask up to a precisely marked volume. The idea sounds simple, but making it precisely true in practice is the entire challenge of volumetric analysis.

Standard solutions split into two categories, and the difference matters. A solution is a primary standard solution if it is made directly from a solid compound that is stable, pure, and has a precisely known molar mass, so the concentration calculated from mass and volume can simply be trusted. Sodium hydroxide, by contrast, cannot usually be made directly into a reliable standard solution: solid NaOH pellets absorb water from the air and react with atmospheric carbon dioxide, so a freshly weighed sample is never quite pure NaOH, and the solution's true concentration always ends up slightly different from what the mass on the label would suggest. A solution like this is called a secondary standard: its approximate concentration is known from preparation, but its exact concentration must be confirmed afterward by titrating it against a primary standard, a process covered in the next section.

Even preparing an approximate secondary standard still leans on molarity directly. Suppose you want roughly 1.000 L of 0.100 M NaOH to use later as a titrant. The mass of NaOH needed is moles times molar mass: 0.100 mol/L x 1.000 L = 0.100 mol, and 0.100 mol x 40.00 g/mol = 4.00 g. In practice you would weigh out approximately 4.0 g of NaOH pellets, dissolve them in water, and dilute to 1.000 L in a volumetric flask, but you would label the resulting solution as only approximately 0.1 M, since the true concentration depends on how much water and carbon dioxide the pellets had already absorbed before they were weighed.

Volumetric flasks themselves are part of what makes a standard solution trustworthy: they are calibrated to hold one exact, precisely marked volume, not to deliver it, the way a burette or pipette is, so diluting up to the etched line is what fixes the denominator in the concentration calculation with high precision. A miscalibrated flask, a solution not fully mixed, or a solute that has not fully dissolved before diluting to the mark are all common sources of error that have nothing to do with the arithmetic and everything to do with technique.

The upshot is that known concentration comes in two trust levels: solutions you can calculate directly and rely on, and solutions you must first check against something more reliable. That second category is exactly why primary standards exist, and why standardizing a solution like NaOH before using it in real analysis is not an optional extra step, it is the step that makes the rest of the analysis valid.
